questions.q: What does the summary call the greatest investment you can make?
a: Yourself and your life experiences
A diversified stock portfolio
A home in a growing city
Your children's education fund
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the best investment is in yourself and in experiences, not in piling up more cash.

questions.q: Why does the summary argue for enjoying certain experiences while you are still young?
a: Some activities are harder to enjoy later in life
Experiences are cheaper earlier in life
Young people have more free time than retirees
Memories fade faster as you age
questions.why: Lesson 1 notes that hiking or boating in your sixties will not feel the same as doing it in your thirties.

questions.q: What does the author recommend regarding money you plan to leave your children?
a: Give part of it while they are young adults
Leave all of it to them after you die
Split it equally with your favourite charity
Hold it in trust until they retire
questions.why: Lesson 2 suggests handing over a comfortable amount earlier so your children can use it when it helps most.

questions.q: What does the summary say about saving money in case of a serious illness?
a: Paying for insurance is cheaper than saving the cash
A large emergency fund beats any insurance policy
Illness costs are too unpredictable to plan for
Only retirees need to worry about medical costs
questions.why: Lesson 2 cites research showing lifelong insurance costs less than stockpiling savings for a possible illness.

questions.q: How does the summary suggest estimating the amount you need for retirement?
a: Multiply yearly living costs by about twenty
Save ten times your current salary
Add up all your monthly expenses for one year
Double whatever you have already invested
questions.why: Lesson 3 says to take what you need to live on each year and multiply it by a round figure such as twenty.
